# parity-fuzz --mode arith baseline: normalized signatures of KNOWN gaps.
# A divergence whose signature is here is allowed; a NEW one fails CI.
# Regenerate: parity-fuzz --mode arith --count N --verify 3  (copy NEW-signature lines).
#
# No known gaps — PROMOTED from informational to a blocking gate.
#
# The class that kept this mode informational was a PARENTHESISED bound in a
# RANGE subscript:
#     arr=(a b c d e); x=2; print -r -- ${arr[(x), 4]}
#     # zsh: b c d        zshrs: a b c d   (the whole 1..4 slice)
#     arr=(a b c d e);      print -r -- ${arr[(1+1), (2+2)]}
#     # zsh: b c d        zshrs: (empty)
#
# The old note here blamed mathevalarg not carrying C's `**ss` out-param, and
# claimed "zshrs splits on the first comma at any paren depth". Both were wrong:
# the port has depth-aware comma tracking in three places, and the subscript
# `(x), 4` is extracted intact. The bug was one branch in the slice-bound
# evaluator (subst.rs eval_idx), which stripped ANY leading `(…)` as a flag
# group:
#     } else {
#         // Separator/word flag (`(s.X.)` etc.) is a no-op for an integer
#         // slice bound; strip it and parse the remainder.
#         effective = &t[close + 1..];
#     }
# For `(x)` there is no flag at all, so the bound became "" and fell back to the
# default 1 — which is why the slice ran from 1 and why `${arr[(1), 3]}`
# "passed" purely by coincidence (stripped → default 1, and 1 was the right
# answer anyway).
#
# c:Src/params.c:1389 only reads `(…)` as flags while the chars are real flags
# (the c:1392-1476 switch: r R k K i I w f e n b p s). c:1477-1482's default arm
#     default:
#       flagerr:
#         num = 1; word = rev = ind = down = keymatch = 0; sep = NULL;
#         s = *str - 1;      /* rewind to before the '(' */
# REWINDS the parse, so an unknown flag char makes the whole group math. That is
# why `${arr[(zz)1]}` reports `bad math expression`, not a flag error. Only the
# RANGE form was affected — a single `${arr[(x)]}` takes a different arm and
# already evaluated as math, which is what made the shape easy to miss.
#
# The generator's subscript arm only ever emitted a SINGLE index, so the mode
# ran clean while the bug was live. It now emits range bounds from both the bare
# and parenthesised vocabularies (`${arr[(x), 4]}` must agree with
# `${arr[x, 4]}`); reverting the fix makes this mode fail, which is the property
# that makes the gate worth having.
#
# OUTPUT RADIX `[#N]` / `[##N]` (math.c convertbase / checkbase): the radix
# arm previously generated only positive operands with plain bases 2/8/16/36/10.
# Three verified-correct dimensions were folded in so a regression fails CI:
#   - NEGATIVE operand: the sign precedes the `B#` prefix (`[#16] -255` ->
#     `-16#FF`, `[##16] -255` -> `-FF`), a distinct output path from positive.
#   - DIGIT GROUPING `_G`: an `_` is inserted every G output digits from the
#     right, and it applies even to base 10 (`[#10_3] 1000000` -> `1_000_000`,
#     `[#16_4] 65535` -> `16#FFFF`).
#   - INVALID BASE out of 2..36: `invalid base (must be 2 to 36 inclusive): N`
#     (folded to stderr via the malformed arm) — a DISTINCT diagnostic from the
#     non-numeric `[#zz]` -> `bad output format specification` (math.c:819).
# All were hand-verified equal on both shells before generating; they are locked
# so a drift in any of the three fails rather than passing silently.
#
# FLOAT DIVISION/MODULO BY ZERO (IEEE-754): unlike the integer path — where a
# zero divisor is UB, masked with `| 1` — float `x/0.0` is DEFINED as ±Inf,
# `0.0/0.0` and `x%0.0` as NaN. `ar_fleaf` never produced a 0.0 divisor, so the
# whole ±Inf/NaN surface went uncompared: the PRINT forms (`Inf`/`-Inf`/`NaN`)
# and the propagation rules (`Inf-Inf` -> NaN, `Inf+Inf` -> Inf, `Inf*0` -> NaN,
# `NaN==NaN` -> 0, `Inf > 1e308` -> 1). The float arm now emits a dedicated
# special-value probe and sometimes forces a `0.0` divisor. All hand-verified
# equal on both shells; locked so a drift in the IEEE-754 output fails CI.
#
# Any divergence here is a regression.
